# Worksheet: your first Julia model code

**~45 minutes**

This is the first worksheet of the workshop and it assumes you have never
written Julia before. Everything here uses the SIR model exactly as the session
presented it. Nothing new is asked of you epidemiologically. What is new is the
Julia: writing a model kernel (the function that computes the rates of change),
broadcasting a calculation over a grid, drawing a figure, and generating random
numbers you can reproduce.

Turning these ingredients into an epidemic curve is the job for the next two sessions.
In this worksheet, we will focus on getting familiar with Julia and writing code.

**How to use this file.** Run cells one at a time with `Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Cells
marked `# TODO` have a line or two for you to complete; everything else runs as
given. Each part ends with `✓` / `✗` lines that check your answer: a `✗` will give
information and the collapsed hint below it will get you moving.

**Parts A and B are the session.** **Part C** goes further if you get there, but not
reaching it is completely fine. Worked solutions will be posted at the end of each
day. Run `git pull` to collect them.

::: {.callout-important}
## The first cell can be slow

The first `using CairoMakie` in a fresh session can take a minute or more while
Julia compiles the plotting stack. It is not frozen, and it only happens once
per session. Later cells will run quickly.
:::

**Coming from R?** Most of what you know transfers.

| R | Julia | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `f <- function(x) x^2` | `f(x) = x^2` | or `function f(x) ... end` |
| `x <- c(1, 2, 3)` | `x = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]` | `1.0` and `1` are different types |
| `v[1]` | `v[1]` | indexing starts at 1, as in R |
| `sapply(v, f)` | `f.(v)` | the dot applies `f` elementwise |
| `x[x < 0.5]` | `x[x .< 0.5]` | comparisons need the dot too |
| `list(a = 1, b = 2)` | `(a = 1, b = 2)` | a named tuple; read fields with `p.a` |
| `TRUE` / `FALSE` | `true` / `false` | lowercase |

The [Julia essentials chapter](../../prerequisites/01-julia-essentials.qmd)
has the full table.

**The REPL is your other window.** Alongside this document you have a Julia
prompt. Besides the ordinary `julia>` prompt it has three other modes. Type the
character at an empty prompt to enter one, `Backspace` to leave:

| Key | Mode | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `?` | help | you want a function's arguments — `?expm1` |
| `]` | package | a package seems missing — `]st` also names the active environment |
| `;` | shell | you need `ls` or `git status` without switching windows |

If `using CairoMakie` fails, that is almost always the project environment not
being active. Check the name in front of the `pkg>` prompt: it should name the
course project, not `@v1.12`. Start Julia with `julia --project=.` from the top
of the repository, or press `]` and run `activate .`. 

Two Julia-specific conventions used throughout the course:

- **Greek letters are ordinary variable names.** We write `β`, `γ`, `λ` because
  they match the equations. At a Julia prompt a backslash and Tab types them:
  `\beta`↹ gives `β`. Inside this Quarto file that completion may not work, see 
  the note below. Plain ASCII names work as well if you prefer them.

- **A trailing `!`** indicates, by convention, that a function modifies one or  
  more of its arguments. For example, `sir_ode!` writes the calculated derivatives 
  directly into the existing `du` array instead of creating a new array.
  This is a Julia naming convention, not something enforced by the language.

::: {.callout-note}
## Greek letters you can copy

`\beta` followed by `Tab` gives `β` at a Julia prompt, but that completion
often may not work inside a Quarto file like this one. There are two ways
to get around it.

**Copy them from here.**

| Symbol | Reads as | At a Julia prompt |
|---|---|---|
| `β` | beta | `\beta` then `Tab` |
| `γ` | gamma | `\gamma` then `Tab` |
| `δ` | delta | `\delta` then `Tab` |
| `λ` | lambda | `\lambda` then `Tab` |

`δt` is two characters: `δ` followed by `t`.

**Or insert them from the command palette.** Install the **Unicode Latex**
extension: open the Extensions panel, search for `unicode-latex`, and install
the one published by *Omer Sheikh*. Then press `Cmd`/`Ctrl`+`Shift`+`P`, type
`unicode`, choose **Unicode: Insert Math Symbol**, type the name of the symbol
you want, and press `Enter`. 

[Setting up](../../setup.qmd#optional-extras) has the install steps in full.
:::

#| label: ws-p01-setup
using CairoMakie

check(name, condition) =

## Part A — writing a model kernel (~15 min)

The session's `sir_ode!` had the in-place signature this course uses everywhere:

```julia
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
```

It writes the rates of change into `du` rather than returning them. SciML also
accepts an out-of-place `f(u, p, t)` that returns a new vector. We stay with the
in-place form as it avoids an allocation on every solver step. You will
use this shape in every remaining session, so it is worth getting familiar with it.

These are the session's equations, unchanged. The force of infection is
$\lambda = \beta c I / N$, and

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\lambda S, \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \lambda S - \gamma I, \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t} = \gamma I.
$$

In the next cell, turn the second and third equations into Julia. The first is
done for you as a worked example.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-p01-a1
p  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]      # S, I, R

function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N        # force of infection, λ = βcI/N
    du[1] = -λ * S                 # dS/dt — worked for you
    du[2] = 0.0     # TODO: replace 0.0 — dI/dt
    du[3] = 0.0     # TODO: replace 0.0 — dR/dt
    return nothing
end

du = zeros(3)
sir_ode!(du, u0, p, 0.0)

check("dI/dt is 2.45 at the baseline", isapprox(du[2], 2.45; atol = 1e-9))
check("dR/dt is 2.50 at the baseline", isapprox(du[3], 2.50; atol = 1e-9))
check("nobody is created or destroyed",
      any(!iszero, du) && isapprox(sum(du), 0.0; atol = 1e-12))
du
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part A

Think of each term as a flow between compartments:

* The infection flow that leaves $S$ must enter $I$.
* The recovery flow that leaves $I$ must enter $R$.

The three lines should sum to zero: every term that leaves one compartment
appears with the opposite sign in another. If the conservation check fails, look
for a sign or a missing term.

The variables `λ`, `S`, and `I` are already available inside the function. 
They are unpacked from the `u` array on the first line of the function.
To access the other parameters (i.e. $\gamma$) we need to access the `p` named tuple as `p.γ`.

`zeros(3)` created `du` before the function ran, and the function filled it in.
That is what "in place" means, and it is why `du` holds your answer after the
call, even though the function returns `nothing`.
:::

### A1. Interpret

These are questions about the Julia, not the epidemiology. 
The block below has a short experiment for each one to help you investigate.

- The function writes `du[2] = ...` rather than `du = [...]`. What would go wrong
  if you built a new array inside the function instead?
- The function ends with `return nothing`, so it hands nothing back. Where did
  your answer end up, and how did it get out?
- The parameters arrived as `p` and you read them with `p.β`. What would break if
  you had used `p[1]` and later reordered the parameters?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Investigate in the Julia REPL

Run each block in the Julia REPL and explain what you observe.
It may help to run it line by line to see what happens at each step.

**1. Building a new array inside a function.**

```julia
function build_new_array(x)
    x = [10.0, 20.0, 30.0]
    return nothing
end

x = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
build_new_array(x)
x
```

Did the `x` outside the function change?

Now the other way round, writing into an element instead of building a new
array. The function has the same shape and still returns `nothing`:

```julia
function write_into_array!(x)
    x[1] = 10.0
    return nothing
end

x = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
write_into_array!(x)
x
```

Which of the two functions changed the caller's array, and which line is
`sir_ode!` doing when it writes `du[1] = ...`? The `!` in the name of the second
one is the convention warning you that it modifies an argument.

**2. Returning and modifying.**

Using the `sir_ode!` you completed above:

```julia
du_trial = fill(NaN, 3)
returned = sir_ode!(du_trial, u0, p, 0.0)

returned
du_trial
```

Which of the two names holds the derivatives?

**3. Reading a parameter by name or by position.**

```julia
p_original  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
p_reordered = (N = 1000.0, γ = 0.25, c = 10.0, β = 0.05)

(p_original.β, p_reordered.β)
(p_original[1], p_reordered[1])
```

Which way of reading $\beta$ still finds the same parameter after the fields are
reordered? Note that the other way raises no error.
:::

> *Your answer here.*

## Part B — the same calculation over a whole grid (~15 min)

A _rate_ describes how often something happens per unit time, whereas a _probability_ describes how
likely it is to happen within a specified time window. If the event occurs at a constant rate ($r$), the probability that it occurs during a window of width ($\delta t$) is:

$$
p(r, \delta t) = 1 - e^{-r\,\delta t},
$$

This probability is often approximated by the simpler expression$r\,\delta t$. 
Here you will investigate when that shortcut is accurate enough and when it is not.

To compare the two expressions across several values of $\delta t$, you could write a loop. 
However, Julia also lets you apply a function element by element using a dot: `f.(v)`, 
which applies `f` to each element of `v`. Dotted operations compile into a single loop 
instead of building a separate array at each step. For a simple numeric vector, this is 
similar to the `sapply(v, f)` function in R.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-p01-b1
rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt)   # numerically stable 1 - exp(-r δt), use ?expm1 to read more about this function

δts = 0.0:0.25:10.0
γ   = 0.25      # the session's recovery rate, per day

linear = γ .* δts    # the shortcut, elementwise — note the dot on the `*`
probs  = Float64[]   # TODO: replace this — rate_to_proportion at rate γ, for every δt in δts

check("one value of each for every δt",
      length(probs) == length(δts) && length(linear) == length(δts))
check("every probability stays between 0 and 1",
      !isempty(probs) && all(0 .<= probs .<= 1))
check("the shortcut escapes [0, 1]", !isempty(linear) && maximum(linear) > 1)
check("the two agree when δt is small",
      length(probs) > 1 && length(linear) > 1 &&
      isapprox(probs[2], linear[2]; rtol = 0.05))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part B

The function `rate_to_proportion` calculates one probability from one rate and one 
window width. You need to apply it once for every value in `δts`. 

You can use dot notation with a function call, just as you used it with the 
multiplication operator in the `linear` expression above.
:::

Now draw them. A figure is built up in pieces: a `Figure` to hold everything, an
`Axis` inside it, then one call per thing you want drawn.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-p01-rate
#| fig-cap: "Probability of at least one event in a window of width δt at rate γ = 0.25, against the linear shortcut γ δt."
fig = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax  = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "window width δt (days)", ylabel = "probability")
hlines!(ax, [1.0]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "probability = 1")
lines!(ax, δts, linear; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "shortcut γ δt")

# TODO: draw the exact curve — lines!(ax, xvalues, yvalues; linewidth = 3, label = "1 - exp(-γ δt)")

axislegend(ax; position = :rb)
ylims!(ax, 0, 2.6)
fig
```

### B1. Interpret

- Up to roughly which $\delta t$ are the two curves hard to tell apart, and at
  approximately what value of $\delta t$ does their difference become noticeable?
- The linear approximation (shortcut) climbs past 1 and keeps going. A probability 
  must remain within the range [0,1], so what does $\gamma\,\delta t$ represent instead?

> *Your answer here.*

## Part C — random numbers you can reproduce (optional)

*Start this only if you have finished Part B.*

Later sessions will use random numbers, but random does not have to mean irreproducible. 
`StableRNG(seed)` creates a local random number generator with a reproducible stream. 
Two freshly created generators with the same seed produce the same sequence of numbers,
and a different seed produces a different sequence. Drawing from a generator also advances
it, so a second draw from the same object continues the stream rather than repeating it,
and only a newly seeded generator starts again from the beginning. Passing this generator explicitly
to `rand` makes the source of randomness visible and prevents the result from depending
on the state of Julia’s default generator.

The force of infection calculated in Part A, $\lambda_0$, is its value at the start of
the day. Feeding $\lambda_0$ into the conversion from Part B with a one-day window gives
the probability that a susceptible person becomes infected during that day, under the
assumption that the force of infection remains fixed at $\lambda_0$.

In a full SIR trajectory, $I$ changes over time, so $\lambda$ changes with it. Holding
$\lambda$ fixed allows us to apply the constant-rate formula directly and focus here on
how probabilities are turned into random events.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-p01-c1
λ0 = p.β * p.c * u0[2] / p.N          # force of infection at the start
p_infect = rate_to_proportion(λ0, 1.0)

# An RNG produces a stream of numbers. Recreating it with the same
# seed restarts that stream from the beginning.
rng_demo = StableRNG(2024)

first_five = rand(rng_demo, 5)
next_five  = rand(rng_demo, 5)

first_five_again = rand(StableRNG(2024), 5)

check("the same seed replays the same stream", first_five == first_five_again)
check("drawing from an RNG advances its stream", first_five != next_five)

function infected_today(rng, n_susceptible, p_infect)
    draws = rand(rng, n_susceptible)
    return 0    # TODO: replace 0 — how many of `draws` came out below p_infect?
end

today = infected_today(StableRNG(1), 990, p_infect)
println("of 990 susceptibles, ", today, " are infected today")

# One million independent trials, to check that their long-run
# frequency approaches p_infect.
fraction = infected_today(StableRNG(2), 1_000_000, p_infect) / 1_000_000
check("the observed fraction matches the probability",
      isapprox(fraction, p_infect; rtol = 0.05))
(; p_infect, fraction, today)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C

Break the task into two steps. First, compare several numbers with one threshold:

```julia
example_draws = [0.2, 0.8, 0.4]
example_draws .< 0.5
```

The dot makes the comparison elementwise, giving one `true` or `false` for each
draw rather than a single answer for the whole array.

Next, see what `count` does with those values:

```julia
count([true, false, true])
```

Now nest the two: count how many values in `draws` came out below `p_infect`.

Leaving the dot off `<` raises a `MethodError`: Julia has no way to compare a
whole array against a single number, so it tells you no method matches rather
than guessing what you meant.
:::

### C1. Interpret

- Run the `today` line again with a few different seeds. Roughly how much does
  the number move? The deterministic model of Part A would give one fixed answer.
  Which is right?
- You saw that drawing from `rng_demo` advanced it, so the next draw carried on
  rather than repeating. Given that, why seed a generator you create yourself
  rather than calling `rand` and setting a global seed once at the top of the
  script?

> *Your answer here.*

## Finish: render your own report

In a terminal, from the top of the repository:

```bash
quarto render worksheets/prerequisites/01-julia-essentials.qmd --to html
```

This starts a new Julia session, runs every cell from the top, and writes an HTML
file next to the worksheet.

It is worth doing because the REPL you have been working in remembers everything
you typed, including lines you tried at the prompt and never put into a cell. A
worksheet can look finished while it is quietly relying on those. Rendering
begins from an empty session and uses only what the file itself contains, so
anything missing shows up now, as an error or a `✗`, rather than later on someone
else's machine. It is the same check worth running on any analysis you intend to
share.
